target: For every nonnegative integer n and every nonempty compact E ⊆ R^n, with I=[0,1] and E×I given the metric induced by the identification (x,t)↦(x,t) in Euclidean R^(n+1), dim_H(E×I)=dim_H(E)+1. Hausdorff dimension uses the pinned convention dim_H(∅)=0.
proof:
Write d=dim_H(E). All metrics below are Euclidean; the product metric is exactly the Euclidean metric under (x,t)↦(x,t)∈R^(n+1). We prove the two inequalities.

Upper bound. Fix any real q>d. Then H^q(E)=0. Given η>0 and a sufficiently small scale δ≤1, choose a countable cover (U_j) of E with 0<r_j:=diam(U_j)≤δ and Σ_j r_j^q<η; one may use positive-radius balls in the Hausdorff cover, so zero-diameter covering sets need not be used. Partition I into at most 2/r_j intervals of length at most r_j (since r_j≤1). The corresponding at most 2/r_j sets U_j×J cover U_j×I; each has Euclidean diameter at most √2 r_j. Thus the sum of their (q+1)-powers of diameters is at most 2(√2)^(q+1) r_j^q. Taking all j gives a cover of E×I of arbitrarily small mesh whose sum of (q+1)-powers is at most 2(√2)^(q+1)η. Since η is arbitrary, H^(q+1)(E×I)=0, hence dim_H(E×I)≤q+1. Letting q decrease to d gives dim_H(E×I)≤d+1.

Lower bound. For every real s with 0≤s<d, apply Frostman's lemma to the nonempty compact set E in R^n to obtain a nonzero finite Borel measure μ supported on E and a constant C such that μ(B(x,r))≤C r^s for every x∈R^n and r>0. Let λ be Lebesgue measure restricted to I and let ν=μ×λ, a nonzero finite Borel measure supported on E×I. For any z=(x,t)∈R^(n+1) and r>0, the Euclidean ball B(z,r) is contained in B(x,r)×(t−r,t+r); consequently ν(B(z,r))≤2C r^(s+1). By the mass distribution principle, dim_H(E×I)≥s+1. Taking the supremum over 0≤s<d yields dim_H(E×I)≥d+1 when d>0. If d=0, choose x₀∈E (possible by nonemptiness) and instead take μ to be the unit point mass at x₀. Then ν=δ_(x₀)×λ is nonzero and ν(B(z,r))≤2r for all z,r, so the same mass distribution principle gives dim_H(E×I)≥1=d+1. Combining both bounds proves the equality.

The correspondence of the displayed product to Euclidean R^(n+1) is isometric: the squared distance between (x,t) and (y,u) is ||x−y||₂²+|t−u|² on both sides, so no change-of-metric dimension result is needed.
